case_study_insert.main_stem: Marrowvale Foods (MVF) is a private limited company in the frozen-food sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2011 by Tomas Vale, it supplies frozen vegetable meals to supermarket chains and cash-and-carry wholesalers and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. MVF plans to invest $640,000 in a new freezing and packing line with recyclable cartons, financed by a $400,000 share issue and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $160,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.20 a unit and a selling price of $10.20, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. MVF faces two problems: quality complaints have risen and waste on the packing line has reached 7%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q1 2025: The freezing line packed 16,500 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.3%, up from 2.1% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 26 to 41 per month. Average delivery time is 4.1 days. Market research of 380 shoppers found that 58% preferred recyclable cartons and 44% would pay up to $0.30 more. A skills audit shows 11 of 38 staff lack on-the-job training on the new freezer; off-the-job training at the local college costs $820 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marrowvale Foods as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (December 2026): (1) The central bank increased the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.2% from $13.10 to $14.04 per hour from April 2026, lifting MVF's wage bill. (3) Wholesale vegetable and packaging costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year, and food-price inflation is 7.4%, while consumer spending on frozen meals grew 2.2%.

questions.question_text: MVF funded part of its freezing-line expansion with a $400,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for MVF of using retained profit instead of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit does not dilute existing ownership or control, so the $240,000 already inside MVF can fund the new freezing line without issuing new shares that would reduce founder Tomas Vale's stake and give outside shareholders a claim on future profits. This matters for a 38-employee private limited company where decisions must stay fast under its hierarchical structure.

Point 2: A share issue involves issue costs and can be hard to place when investor appetite is weak, whereas retained profit has no flotation expense and is immediately available. Using it keeps the $640,000 expansion within internal resources and leaves MVF's $160,000 a year of fixed costs and its developing $400,000 share proceeds free for other uses, such as absorbing the 11.3% rise in vegetable and packaging costs without raising the $10.20 selling price.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to MVF's ownership, financing and costs.

questions.question_text: MVF is launching frozen meals in recyclable cartons. Consider national television advertising, trade fairs and exhibitions, or social media influencer marketing. Which should MVF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign would create rapid brand awareness for the new recyclable-carton meals across the supermarket chains that stock MVF. However, airtime is extremely expensive for a 38-staff frozen-food firm that has just committed $640,000 to a freezing line, and much of the audience would never see the product in the cash-and-carry wholesalers it supplies, so spending would be poorly targeted.

Trade fairs and exhibitions: These let MVF demonstrate the cartons directly to supermarket buyers and wholesale customers, generate firm orders and gather feedback on the 3.3% defect-rate concerns. They are far cheaper than television and fit a business-to-business selling model. The limits are narrow reach to the trade rather than final shoppers, high staff time, and only occasional timing, which may not sustain a launch across 16,500 units a quarter.

Social media influencer marketing: Recipe and family-food influencers can show the frozen meals being cooked and reach precisely the 58% of 380 surveyed shoppers who prefer recyclable cartons and the 44% who would pay up to $0.30 more. Engagement is measurable, cost per contact is low, and the message can run continuously. Results depend on influencer credibility and build more slowly than TV, but the fit with the research segment is strong.

Recommendation: MVF should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the research-identified shoppers who value recyclable cartons, costs far less than television, and reaches final buyers that trade fairs cannot, while supporting the $10.20 price. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 38-person business funding a $640,000 line; trade fairs are rejected as too narrow and occasional to sustain volume. MVF should complement influencers with a small presence at key trade fairs to win listings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to MVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in MVF's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in MVF's context and recommends influencer marketing with clear reasons for rejecting television and trade fairs.

questions.question_text: MVF's quality complaints have risen and waste has reached 7%. Explain two benefits for MVF of using autocratic leadership to improve quality on the packing line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets MVF's manager set clear quality standards and enforce inspection routines quickly on the new freezer, which is valuable when the defect rate has risen to 3.3% and complaints climbed from 26 to 41 per month. In a hierarchical structure of 38 staff, decisive instructions reduce confusion and stop faulty packs reaching supermarket chains, protecting the $640,000 investment.

Point 2: Tight central control can cut the 7% packing-line waste by specifying exact filling settings and requiring checks, raising output from the 70,000-unit plan and defending the $5.00 contribution per unit against 11.3% input inflation. It also means the $820-per-employee off-the-job training budget can be directed to the skillsMVF actually needs, rather than leaving 11 untrained staff to improvise on the freezer.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development linked to MVF's complaints, defect rate, waste and training.

questions.question_text: MVF must upskill 11 staff on the new freezer. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should MVF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the freezer is tailored to MVF's own equipment and quality checks, costs no course fees, and keeps the 11 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 16,500-unit quarterly output and the effort needed to reverse the 3.3% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that trainers are working supervisors whose own duties suffer, bad habits may spread, and there is no formal certificate for supermarket audits.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $820 per employee provides structured, current skills and a recognised certificate for all 11 staff, costing $9,020 in total — reasonable against the $640,000 expansion. However, it takes staff off the line when complaints are already high, reducing short-term capacity, and generic content may not match MVF's exact freezer settings, so on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: MVF should choose on-the-job training first, then send a small number of senior operators for the college certificate. On-the-job training is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while the defect rate is 3.3% and waste is 7%; full off-the-job training is rejected because $9,020 and eleven absences would disrupt supermarket deliveries at a critical launch, and the course can be added once the freezer is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited application to MVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in MVF's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in MVF's context with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and quality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MVF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 32,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 70,000-unit output; pricing against $160,000 fixed costs; share-issue and dividend feasibility for the $640,000 line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $7.49 to attack 7% waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate answer in each calculation; 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $160,000 ÷ ($10.20 − $5.20) = $160,000 ÷ $5.00 = 32,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 32,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.20 − $5.20 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MVF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 32,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 70,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 38,000 units, to see how much demand could fall before the new freezer loses money.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.00 lets MVF test a price promotion: a $0.30 discount would leave $4.70, showing the extra volume needed to cover $160,000 of fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the sales target that must be met before the $400,000 share issue can deliver acceptable returns, supporting the board's $640,000 investment decision.
4. Unit cost of $7.49 ($160,000 ÷ 70,000 units + $5.20) gives a quarterly benchmark to isolate the 7% packing-line waste and the 3.3% defect rate, guiding talks with packaging suppliers amid 11.3% input inflation.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MVF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MVF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.20 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.40 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $64,000 inventories + $92,000 trade receivables + $36,000 cash = $192,000; 2025 current assets = $68,000 + $120,000 + $50,000 = $238,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $160,000 and $170,000 gives 1.20 and 1.40. Excluding inventories, $128,000 ÷ $160,000 = 0.80 in 2024 and $170,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.00 in 2025.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has improved. The broader measure rose from 1.20 to 1.40 because current assets grew from $192,000 to $238,000 faster than current liabilities, which rose only from $160,000 to $170,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.80 to 1.00, so MVF now covers its short-term debts without depending on selling frozen stock — useful while it spends $640,000 on a new freezing line. However, trade receivables jumped from $92,000 to $120,000, locking up cash that could fund the 7.2% wage rise; if supermarket chains pay late, the improvement may reverse, and inventories rose to $68,000, which could mean slower-moving stock.

Conclusion: MVF's financial position has improved. Both measures show stronger liquidity and the stricter measure no longer relies on inventories. The main concern is rising receivables, so MVF should tighten credit control before committing more of the $400,000 share proceeds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with some contextual analysis.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations plus detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MVF of using recyclable cartons for its frozen meals.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable cartons appeal to the 58% of 380 surveyed shoppers who prefer them and the 44% who would pay up to $0.30 more, helping MVF defend its $5.00 contribution per unit while vegetable and packaging costs rise 11.3%. The environmental positioning also strengthens its pitch to supermarket chains for listings on the $640,000 freezing line.

Disadvantage: Recyclable carton board generally costs more than standard packaging, pushing up the $5.20 variable cost per unit unless the whole $0.30 premium is secured. If the cartons perform poorly in frozen storage they could worsen the 3.3% defect rate and the 7% packing-line waste, adding cost just as MVF is trying to cut quality complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using MVF's research, costs and quality data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in input costs will affect MVF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The insert shows MVF financed the $640,000 expansion through a $400,000 share issue and $240,000 retained profit, with no bank loan, so there is no existing debt on which interest rises. The effect is indirect: future borrowing for the frozen meals launch becomes more expensive, and consumers may cut discretionary spending. Because MVF has no stated loan, no interest saving or charge can be quantified without inventing debt, so this is judged qualitatively and is the least immediate of the three.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, to $14.04 per hour): MVF has a workforce of 38 in packing and freezing roles, so this raises its wage bill and cannot be avoided. No hours or individual pay rates are given, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible test is productivity — 70,000 units ÷ 38 staff is about 1,842 units per worker, meaning the rise is affordable only if that productivity holds or output grows, otherwise unit labour cost erodes the $5.00 contribution.

Input cost inflation (11.3% vegetables and packaging): The insert never breaks down the $5.20 variable cost, so only a bound is honest — if the entire variable cost rose 11.3% it would add 11.3% × $5.20 = $0.59 per unit, or about $41,300 a year at 70,000 units. Even a smaller pass-through would squeeze contribution, and this recurs on every unit while the 7.4% food-price inflation may limit MVF's ability to raise price.

Conclusion: The 11.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 70,000 units and directly erodes the contribution behind the $640,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise does not touch any stated debt and the wage rise can partly be offset by productivity.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to MVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on MVF's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
